lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Flush’s ecstatic welcome shows how much home and routine mean to her, a vivid early moment only they would recognise.

lines.text: Now I will kiss you, dearest: used you to divine that at the very beginning, I have sometimes shortened the visit in order to arrive at the time of taking your hand?
lines.note: Robert’s confession that he sometimes shortened visits to reach the moment of taking her hand captures his private devotion.

lines.text: May God bless you, dearest beloved, I love, love you!
lines.note: A direct, unmistakable declaration of love from Elizabeth, grounding the poem in their own words.

lines.text: How I miss you, and long for Friday.
lines.note: Elizabeth’s plain ‘How I miss you’ speaks directly to the occasion and their growing separation.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: The sudden loss of Flush is one of the most concrete shared crises in the letters.

lines.text: Poor Flush—how sorry I am for you, my Ba!
lines.note: Robert’s sympathy for Flush shows him entering Elizabeth’s world and its small, beloved creatures.

lines.text: This is the first time since we met at the beginning, that a whole week, from a Sunday to a Saturday, has gone by without a day for us.
lines.note: Robert marks the unusual week without a meeting, making the absence itself part of their story.

lines.text: And smiling to myself I was, both last night and this morning, at your phrase about the ‘business’ to be talked by the ‘grave man and woman’; understanding your precaution against all unlawful jesting!—jesters forbidden in the protocol!
lines.note: Elizabeth’s playful recognition of Robert’s ‘grave man and woman’ phrase shows their private jesting about marriage.

lines.text: Dearest, you are a prophet, I suppose—there can be no denying it.
lines.note: Elizabeth calling Robert a prophet echoes their running pattern of prediction and surprise.

lines.text: Dearest, I write one word, and have one will which is yours.
lines.note: Her ‘one will which is yours’ is a turning point: she places her will with his as the plan becomes real.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: After the wedding day, Elizabeth’s relieved ‘all is safe so far’ carries the breathless aftermath they both lived.

lines.text: Thank you a thousand times for the note, my own Ba.
lines.note: Robert’s gratitude for her note after the marriage shows how deeply he felt her effort and proof of love.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: On the eve of leaving, Elizabeth’s thought that she will have Robert only to love her closes the arc of separation and reunion.
